CausalChain: Chronic liver disease (NAFLD, hepatitis) → upregulation of de novo lipogenesis (via FASN, SCD) → increased synthesis of sphingolipids and accumulation of S1P → S1P secretion leads to activation of oncogenic and immunosuppressive pathways (through S1PR-mediated YAP/PI3K/AKT signaling) → enhanced lipid droplet formation can sequester lipids including S1P, thus reducing its extracellular bioavailability → reduced S1P signaling may restore antitumor immunity and impair tumor progression.
Hypothesis: Enhancing lipid droplet formation in hepatocellular carcinoma cells will sequester sphingosine‐1‐phosphate, thereby decreasing its extracellular signaling that promotes immunosuppression and oncogenic pathway activation, ultimately leading to improved tumor immune surveillance and reduced tumor progression.
Abstract: In hepatocellular carcinoma, deregulated lipid metabolism, characterized by increased de novo lipogenesis and altered sphingolipid synthesis, produces bioactive lipids such as sphingosine‐1‐phosphate (S1P) that promote oncogenic signaling and contribute to an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Recent findings suggest that lipid droplets, as intracellular lipid reservoirs, can sequester lipid species and thereby potentially affect the availability of signaling molecules. We propose a novel hypothesis whereby enhancing lipid droplet formation in HCC cells may functionally sequester S1P, reducing its release into the tumor milieu. This in turn would attenuate S1P‐mediated activation of proliferative and immunosuppressive pathways and may restore effective antitumor immune responses. Here, we describe a causal chain linking chronic liver disease‐induced lipogenesis, accumulation of S1P and its oncogenic influence, and the modulatory role of lipid droplets in mediating the extracellular pool of S1P.
